desc:
An undirected graph has n nodes labelled 0 to n - 1. Each edges[i] = [a, b, w] is an edge of positive weight w.

A simple cycle visits at least three different nodes, returns to its start and never repeats a node or an edge. Return the smallest total weight of any simple cycle in the graph, or -1 if the graph has no cycle at all.

Example: n = 5, edges = [[0,1,1],[1,2,2],[2,3,3],[3,0,4],[0,2,10]]. The square 0-1-2-3 weighs 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10, the triangle 0-1-2 weighs 1 + 2 + 10 = 13 and the triangle 0-2-3 weighs 10 + 3 + 4 = 17, so the answer is 10. A graph that is a tree (for instance only the edges [[0,1,1],[1,2,1]]) has answer -1.
constraints: edges[i] = [a, b, w] with 0 ≤ a, b < n, a ≠ b and 1 ≤ w ≤ 1,000
No two edges join the same pair of nodes
hints: A cycle through an edge (u, v) is that edge plus a different route from u back to v. For one edge, how would you find the cheapest such route?
Brute force: for every edge, remove it and run Dijkstra between its endpoints, cost O(E · E log n). Floyd-Warshall can do better by thinking of the highest-numbered node k of a cycle.

During Floyd-Warshall, before allowing k as an intermediate node, d[i][j] is the shortest i-j route using only nodes below k. For all i ≠ j below k with edges to k, the cycle i ~ j - k - i has weight d[i][j] + w(j,k) + w(k,i). Take the minimum over all k, i, j, then update d with k.
editorial: Order the nodes by label and look at the largest-labelled node k on a lightest cycle. Its two cycle neighbours i and j have smaller labels, and the rest of the cycle is a simple route from i to j that only uses nodes below k. So the cycle weight is at least d_k[i][j] + w(i,k) + w(k,j) where d_k is the shortest-distance table that Floyd-Warshall holds just before it processes k (intermediates restricted to nodes below k). Conversely every such candidate corresponds to a real simple cycle: the shortest i-j route avoids k, is simple, and together with the two edges to k it closes into a cycle with at least three nodes. Therefore the answer is the minimum candidate over all k and all unordered pairs i, j of neighbours of k with labels below k.

Evaluate the candidates for k first, then relax all pairs through k as usual. The candidate loops cost O(n3/6) in total and the relaxations O(n3), with O(n2) space. Do not simply use the full shortest-path matrix: d[i][i] is 0, and going i → j → i along the same edge is not a cycle. That is why distinct nodes and the 'strictly below k' restriction (which keeps the i-j route from using k or the same edges) are essential. An alternative is O(n · E log n) by removing each edge in turn and running Dijkstra between its endpoints.
